nameStory: Silver wormwood gets its shimmering name from the silvery-white hairs that coat its leaves, giving the whole plant a frosted appearance that catches sunlight beautifully. The 'wormwood' part comes from the traditional use of plants in this genus to expel intestinal worms, though you definitely shouldn't try this at home! Its scientific name 'ludoviciana' is simply the fancy Latin way of saying 'from Louisiana,' where early botanists first formally described this widespread prairie native.
description: Silver wormwood is a sturdy perennial herb that grows 1-4 feet tall, spreading by underground runners to form colonies. Its most striking feature is the silvery-white coating of fine hairs that gives the entire plant a frosted, almost ghostly appearance. The narrow, deeply-lobed leaves look almost lacy, and in late summer it produces tiny, inconspicuous yellowish flower heads clustered along the stems. This is a true prairie plant that brings a touch of the American West to New England gardens and wild spaces.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, deeply-lobed leaves covered in dense silvery-white hairs that feel soft and fuzzy to the touch, giving them an almost velvet-like texture and distinctive frosted appearance

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms colonies through underground runners, creating patches of silvery foliage that stand 1-4 feet tall with multiple upright stems from the base

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous yellowish flower heads clustered in narrow spikes along the upper stems, lacking the showy petals typical of other daisy family members

idTips.label: Scent
idTips.description: Crush a leaf and smell the distinctive sage-like, slightly bitter aroma that's characteristic of the wormwood genus

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Sturdy, upright stems also covered in the same silvery-white hairs as the leaves, giving the entire plant a uniform frosted appearance

habitat: In New England, silver wormwood is most commonly found in disturbed soils, along roadsides, in abandoned fields, and in well-drained garden settings where it has escaped cultivation. It thrives in full sun and tolerates poor, dry soils better than most plants. While native to the western prairies, it has established itself in scattered locations throughout New England, particularly in areas with sandy or gravelly soil.

seasonality.spring: New silvery shoots emerge from underground runners, quickly developing the characteristic frosted foliage that makes identification easy even when young.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full height with lush silvery foliage at its most striking. Late summer brings the small, clustered flower heads that bloom into early fall.
seasonality.fall: Flowers mature and produce tiny seeds, while the silvery foliage may begin to fade but often remains recognizable well into the season.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground portions die back completely, leaving only the underground runner system to survive New England's harsh winters.

funFact: Silver wormwood is the plant traditionally used to make absinthe's less potent American cousin - it contains some of the same compounds that gave the famous 'Green Fairy' liqueur its reputation, though in much smaller amounts that won't cause hallucinations!
confusionNotes: The silvery, fuzzy foliage makes this nearly unmistakable among New England plants, but gardeners might confuse it with dusty miller or lamb's ear before it flowers. Remember: silver wormwood has deeply-lobed, narrow leaves with that distinctive sage-like smell when crushed, while dusty miller has broader, less divided leaves and lamb's ear has much larger, tongue-shaped leaves.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Louisiana wormwood,' this plant is actually native to the western prairies and was just first scientifically described from Louisiana. Don't let the many common names fool you - white sagebrush, prairie sage, and western mugwort all refer to this same silvery beauty that's made its way east.
compareHints: Silver wormwood stands out from its New England Artemisia relatives by its intensely silvery-white appearance - common mugwort has green tops to its leaves, while hoary mugwort is more coastal and has different leaf shapes. The silvery coating is so dense on silver wormwood that both leaf surfaces look nearly white, unlike the green-and-white contrast seen in other local wormwoods. Its colony-forming habit through runners also distinguishes it from the more clumping growth of most other Artemisia species in our region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's Artemisia species, common mugwort is the tallest and most common, with the most deeply divided leaves.
Unlike common mugwort which has green leaves with white undersides, hoary mugwort is silvery-white all over and much more compact.
Among New England's Artemisia species, field sagewort stands out for its preference for the driest, sandiest soils and its exceptionally finely-divided silvery leaves.
Among New England's wormwoods, Sweet Annie is unique for its sweet fragrance and annual growth habit - most other wormwoods are perennial and smell bitter.
Absinthe wormwood is much more silvery and aromatic than common mugwort, which has green leaves with white undersides.
Among New England's Artemisia species, biennial wormwood has the most finely divided leaves - much more delicate-looking than the broader-lobed common mugwort or the silvery hoary mugwort.
